title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding

Title:Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Low-precision training reduces computation but introduces additional rounding error. We theoretically study how stochastic rounding (SR) affects prediction risk as model size, training time, and precision change. We consider a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian data with power-law spectra. At each SGD step, the features used in forward and backward computations are rounded independently. We prove matched upper and lower bounds on prediction error for the final model and for uniform parameter averaging, with general learning-rate and precision schedules chosen before training. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute, and we identify model sizes and training times that achieve this optimal-compute scaling. Rounding only the forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it. Averaging parameters can change which computation needs higher precision and when higher precision is useful. Our results also give bit requirements for a given accuracy tolerance and show how backward rounding can change learning-rate schedule design. At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the additional SR-induced error. Model simulations illustrate these tradeoffs, and experiments with an MLP and a small transformer examine rounding choices beyond the theoretical model.

report.summary: New theory shows how stochastic rounding, model size, training time, and bit precision jointly determine SGD prediction error, revealing when lower precision can improve compute efficiency.
report.background: Low-precision training is now central to scaling AI models: FP16, BF16 and FP8 cut memory and compute costs, but rounding errors can destabilize training. Most hardware uses round-to-nearest, while stochastic rounding (SR) randomizes the error direction and is theoretically better for unbiased accumulation. Previous scaling laws mostly assume exact arithmetic or empirical heuristics, leaving unclear how bit width should be allocated across forward and backward passes, model size and training duration. This paper builds a theoretical bridge, asking where (forward vs backward), when (schedule) and how many bits should be used to minimize prediction risk under a fixed compute budget.
key_points: The authors analyze a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian data with power-law spectra. They prove matching upper and lower bounds on prediction error for both the final model and uniform parameter averaging, allowing arbitrary learning-rate and precision schedules set before training. This makes the results a clean scaling-law benchmark for stochastic rounding rather than a single empirical observation.

Rounding only forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it. Intuitively, backward rounding perturbs gradient updates and interacts with learning-rate choices, so it carries a different cost than forward rounding. This suggests precision allocation should be asymmetric: saving bits in forward computation may be safer than aggressive backward quantization.

Parameter averaging changes which computation needs higher precision and when higher precision is worthwhile. With constant learning rates and averaging, the paper derives how minimum prediction error scales with compute and identifies model sizes and training times that attain optimal-compute scaling. Averaging is therefore not just a convenience; it alters the precision tradeoff.

At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction if the saved compute is reinvested in a larger model or longer training, and that benefit outweighs extra SR-induced error. This is the key counterintuitive result: fewer bits are not automatically worse, because scaling laws couple precision with model size and duration.

The theory yields bit requirements for a target accuracy tolerance and shows backward rounding can change learning-rate schedule design. Simulations illustrate the tradeoffs, and MLP/transformer experiments test rounding choices beyond the theoretical model, hinting at practical precision-placement rules but not yet universal prescriptions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper argues against treating bit width as a single global knob. Precision should be co-designed with model size, training horizon, learning-rate schedule and parameter averaging. Hardware and compiler teams may need finer-grained controls for forward vs backward rounding. For developers, the practical lesson is to test asymmetric precision budgets and SR-aware schedules, especially when using FP8 or low-bit training. For regular users, cheaper and more efficient training could translate into lower serving costs and more capable models, but the benefits depend on engineering the precision tradeoff correctly; the results are theoretical and need validation at frontier scale.
report.tools: Readers can follow low-precision training through PyTorch AMP/FSDP, NVIDIA Transformer Engine for FP8, DeepSpeed, bitsandbytes, and JAX/Flax. For stochastic rounding specifically, watch custom CUDA/Triton kernels and quantization libraries that expose rounding modes; most mainstream frameworks still default to round-to-nearest. The paper's simulations are a useful blueprint for reproducing forward-vs-backward precision experiments on small MLPs and transformers.
